opening: In Chapter 6, we saw that applying a reversible function gate \(U_f\) to a uniform superposition of inputs evaluates \(f(x)\) on every bit string simultaneously—yet measuring the register yields only one random pair \((x, f(x))\), and any attempt to interfere different input branches is blocked whenever the target qubit retains a record of \(f(x)\). How, then, can a quantum computation ever outperform a classical one?
opening_continuation: To compare quantum and classical algorithms on equal footing, we introduce the query (or black-box) model, where the cost of an algorithm is measured by how many times it consults the function \(f\). We pose the simplest global question: for a one-bit Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}\), is \(f\) constant (\(f(0)=f(1)\)) or balanced (\(f(0)\ne f(1)\))? Classically, answering with certainty requires two queries. In this chapter, we show why querying \(U_f\) with the target qubit in \(\ket{0}\) fails to separate the two cases, and how preparing the target in the bit-flip eigenstate \(\ket{-} = (\ket{0}-\ket{1})/\sqrt{2}\) eliminates the target record while transferring each output \(f(x)\) into a phase factor \((-1)^{f(x)}\) on the input register—a mechanism called phase kickback. A final Hadamard gate converts that relative sign into a deterministic answer in just one query: Deutsch's algorithm.
intro_continuation: How does a single quantum query determine whether \(f(0) = f(1)\) without ever revealing the individual bit \(f(0)\) or \(f(1)\)? By preparing the target qubit in \(\ket{-}\), flipping the target when \(f(x)=1\) leaves the target state completely unchanged in \(\ket{-}\) while multiplying the \(\ket{x}\) branch by \(-1\). Because no path record remains in the target, the two input branches interfere cleanly at a final Hadamard gate—producing outcome 0 when the signs agree and outcome 1 when the signs are opposite.
